What perspectives are: A perspective is a lens for explaining behavior. Psychology uses seven of them, and the same behavior can be explained through several at once. This section names the idea; the next one goes through each lens.
The seven perspectives: Learn each perspective by its key word. Psychodynamic: the unconscious and childhood. Cognitive: thoughts. Behavioral: learning and rewards. Humanistic: potential and free will. Biological: genes, brain chemistry and hormones. Evolutionary: survival and reproduction. Sociocultural: culture.
Applying perspectives: Test questions describe a behavior and ask which perspective explains it. Look for the key word in each explanation (unconscious, thoughts, rewards, potential, chemistry, ancestors, culture) and match it to its perspective, as in the Suzanne example.
Why psychology needs research: Psychology relies on research because intuition is unreliable. Three biases distort it: hindsight bias (I knew it all along), overconfidence (thinking you know more than you do), and misunderstanding probability (seeing patterns in random events).
The scientific method: Research follows seven steps, starting with observation and ending with replication. A theory explains observations; a hypothesis is a testable prediction. Operational definitions say exactly how each variable is measured, which is what lets other researchers replicate a study.
Types of research: There are three kinds of research. Descriptive research describes behavior, correlational research finds relationships, and experimental research tests cause and effect. Only experiments can show cause.
Descriptive methods: The three descriptive methods each trade something off. A case study goes deep on one person but may not apply to others. Naturalistic observation sees real behavior but people may notice the observer. A survey collects a lot of data fast but depends on honest self-reports.
Correlation: A correlation shows how two variables move together: positive (same direction), negative (opposite directions) or zero. The coefficient's closeness to +1 or −1 shows strength; the sign only shows direction. Two rules to remember: positive doesn't mean good, and correlation doesn't prove causation.
Experiments: An experiment studies a sample drawn from a population, ideally a random, representative one. The experimental group gets the independent variable (what the researcher changes), the control group doesn't, and the dependent variable is what gets measured. A confounding variable is anything else that could explain the result.
Problems with research: Many things can distort results: expectations (placebo effect), being watched (Hawthorne effect), wanting to look good (social desirability bias), unrepresentative samples (sampling bias), and how questions are worded. Learn to name each problem from a short scenario.
Ethics: APA guidelines protect participants: participation is voluntary, people give informed consent before and are debriefed after, information stays confidential, there's no long-term harm, animals are treated humanely, and an institution must approve the study first.
Descriptive statistics: Descriptive statistics organize and summarize data. A frequency distribution shows how often each score appears, and a histogram is the bar graph that displays it.
Central tendency: Three ways to find the center: the mean (average), the median (middle score in order) and the mode (most common score). Percentile rank tells what percentage of scores fall below yours.
Variation: Variation is how spread out the scores are. The range is highest minus lowest; standard deviation shows how much scores vary around the mean. On a normal curve about 68% of scores fall within 1 standard deviation and about 95% within 2.
Skewed data: An outlier can pull a distribution out of shape. In positive skew the tail points right; in negative skew it points left. The mean always follows the tail, while a symmetrical distribution has mean = median = mode.
Inferential statistics: Inferential statistics ask whether results apply beyond the sample. Representative samples, bigger samples and more estimates are better; a meta-analysis combines many studies. A result is statistically significant when p ≤ .05, and effect size tells how strong the effect is.
